templates.name: Modifier placement: past participial opener (incl. Compared with that of)
Subject-verb agreement, relative pronoun or possessive inside subject
Plural vs possessive nouns: one- or two-slot spelling grid
Finite vs nonfinite, finite second or subordinate verb
Finite vs nonfinite, finite main verb

items.subtype: Modifier placement: preposition + passive gerund opener (Instead of being cast ... and then fitted into place), passage-final clause; the obvious noun (the stone blocks) fits only half of the opener
items.passage: Archaeologists studying Pumapunku, a monumental temple complex constructed around 600 CE at Tiwanaku in present-day Bolivia, have long admired the precision of its andesite and sandstone masonry, in which adjoining blocks were secured with metal clamps. Instead of being cast in molds and then fitted into place, ______
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: the stone blocks were joined by clamps that workers poured, molten, into I-shaped sockets cut in them.
many of the clamps were poured, molten, into I-shaped sockets cut in neighboring blocks.
the clamps’ installation often involved pouring them, molten, into I-shaped sockets cut in neighboring blocks.
there were many clamps poured, molten, into I-shaped sockets cut in neighboring blocks.
items.explanation: The opening phrase describes something that was not “cast in molds and then fitted into place,” which can only be the metal clamps. Choice B places “many of the clamps” immediately after the phrase, so the phrase correctly describes the clamps.

A.recipe: wrong noun as subject (W): the obvious noun keeps every fact
A.why_wrong: “The stone blocks” follows the phrase, so the sentence illogically says that the blocks were not cast in molds; the blocks were cut, and it is the clamps that could have been cast.

C.recipe: possessive on the right noun (P): the clamps’ installation
C.why_wrong: The subject is “installation,” not the clamps, so the sentence illogically says that the installation was not cast in molds and fitted into place.

D.why_wrong: The word “there” follows the phrase, leaving the phrase without a logical noun to describe.

items.notes: Subject: history and archaeology (Pumapunku at Tiwanaku, Bolivia; metal clamps poured into I-shaped sockets). No named researchers. Options 13 to 17 words; key not the longest.
band7_moves: the opener has two halves and the obvious noun fits the second (blocks are “fitted into place”) but not the first (blocks are not “cast in molds”), so the student must test the whole phrase
hardest distractor (A) starts with the obvious noun of the passage, the stone blocks, and keeps every fact
a possessive built on the right noun (C, “the clamps’ installation”), as “commercial plastics’ two associated problems” in 37e5c794, so seeing “clamps” right after the comma is not enough
passage-final full-clause options, recipes W, P (possessive on the right noun), E

band7.why: Plain-thing key as in the one band-7 prep-gerund official (37e5c794); after the fix two distractors are built on the right noun (possessive, expletive) and A keeps every fact with the obvious noun, which fits half the opener (blocks are fitted into place, not cast). Passage 48 words, above the short model but at the hard-tier median.

fixes: hardened: C was “Tiwanaku’s metalworkers” (ruled out by one fact); now the possessive “the clamps’ installation,” recipe P as in 37e5c794

items.subtype: Modifier placement: preposition + gerund opener (By following), passage-final clause; plain agent key
items.passage: Ming dynasty geographer Xu Xiake devoted more than three decades to traveling across China, recording meticulous observations of rivers, caves, and limestone formations in his diaries. Classical texts had long identified the Min River as the main source of the Yangtze. By following the Jinsha River deep into the mountains of the southwest, ______
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: Xu’s conclusion was that the Jinsha, not the Min, is the Yangtze’s true upper course.
the Jinsha, rather than the Min, was shown by Xu to be the Yangtze’s true upper course.
it was Xu who concluded that the Jinsha, not the Min, is the Yangtze’s true upper course.
Xu concluded that the Jinsha, not the Min, is the Yangtze’s true upper course.
items.explanation: The person who followed the Jinsha River deep into the mountains was Xu. Choice D places “Xu” immediately after the opening phrase, so the phrase correctly describes him.

A.why_wrong: The subject is “Xu’s conclusion,” so the sentence illogically says that a conclusion followed the river into the mountains.

B.recipe: passive that leaves the wrong noun as subject (V)
B.why_wrong: “The Jinsha” follows the phrase, so the sentence illogically says that the river followed itself into the mountains.

C.why_wrong: The word “it” follows the phrase, so the phrase has no logical noun to describe; the person who did the following must be the subject.

items.notes: Subject: history of geography (Ming geographer Xu Xiake traced the Yangtze to the Jinsha rather than the Min). Real figure, known; only his core argument is stated. Options 14 to 17 words; key the shortest, as in 3.15.

band7.why: Plain agent key with P, V and E distractors, the recipe of band-6 dfbf5d33; a strong band 6 as targeted.

items.subtype: Modifier placement: past participial opener (Inferred from), passage-final clause; right subject is a property (the diet of P. boisei)
items.passage: Because of its massive jaws and enormous, flattened molars, the hominin Paranthropus boisei was nicknamed “Nutcracker Man” shortly after its discovery in 1959, on the assumption that it subsisted on hard nuts and seeds. Inferred from carbon isotopes preserved in its fossilized tooth enamel, however, ______
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: the diet of P. boisei consisted mostly of grasses and sedges, plants that are tough but not hard.
P. boisei ate mostly grasses and sedges, plants that are tough but not hard.
the fossils of P. boisei show that it ate mostly grasses and sedges, plants that are tough but not hard.
there is evidence that P. boisei ate mostly grasses and sedges, plants that are tough but not hard.
items.explanation: What is “inferred from carbon isotopes preserved in its fossilized tooth enamel” is what the species ate, not the species itself: a diet is exactly what scientists infer from such chemical evidence. Choice A places “the diet of P. boisei” immediately after the opening phrase, so the phrase correctly describes the diet.

B.recipe: wrong noun as subject (W): the obvious noun keeps every fact
B.why_wrong: “P. boisei” follows the phrase, so the sentence illogically says that the hominin itself was inferred from the carbon in its teeth.

C.recipe: wrong noun as subject (W) in the key’s own shape (the X of P. boisei)
C.why_wrong: “The fossils of P. boisei” follows the phrase, so the sentence illogically says that the fossils were inferred from carbon isotopes; the fossils are the evidence, not what was inferred from it.

D.why_wrong: The word “there” follows the phrase, leaving the phrase without a logical noun to describe.

items.notes: Subject: natural science (Paranthropus boisei, “Nutcracker Man”; carbon isotopes in tooth enamel point to a diet of grasses and sedges). No named researchers. Options 14 to 19 words; key not the longest.
band7_moves: property key: only what the hominin ate can be “inferred from the carbon in its fossilized tooth enamel,” so the right subject is “the diet of P. boisei” (the Y of X, as the HHI score of a market in fced396a)
hardest distractor (B) starts with the obvious noun and keeps every fact
a second wrong subject in the key’s own shape (“the fossils of P. boisei”), so spotting the “the X of Y” option is not enough; the student must ask which property can be inferred
fresh opener (Inferred from) instead of “Compared with that of”; recipes W, W, E

band7.why: Property key (“the diet of P. boisei”) as in fced396a and 2dd1b8bf; B keeps every fact with the obvious noun, and after the fix C mirrors the key’s shape. Passage 46 words, above the short models but at the hard-tier median.

fixes: hardened: C was “researchers have concluded” (the only other agent-like option, ruled out at a glance, and it left the key the only “the X of Y” phrase); now “the fossils of P. boisei show,” same shape as the key

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement: singular possessor before a plural head (The book’s ... portrayals), intervener with its own singular verb
items.passage: John Okada’s only novel, No-No Boy (1957), follows Ichiro Yamada, a Japanese American returning to Seattle after imprisonment for resisting the military draft during World War II. The book’s unflinching portrayals of Ichiro’s anguish and of a community that remains bitterly divided over his decision ______ it a lasting place in Asian American literature.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject of the second sentence is the plural noun “portrayals,” not “book’s,” “anguish,” “community” or “decision.” The plural verb “have won” agrees with it.

A.why_wrong: “Has won” is singular and does not agree with the plural subject “portrayals.”

B.why_wrong: “Wins” is singular and does not agree with the plural subject “portrayals.”

D.why_wrong: “Is winning” is singular and does not agree with the plural subject “portrayals.”

items.notes: Subject: literature (John Okada’s No-No Boy). Real work, known; plot facts only.
band7_moves: singular possessor before a plural head (“The book’s ... portrayals”), as “her book’s musings” in f10b7ce4
singular nouns between head and blank (anguish, community, decision, plus the possessor Ichiro’s) and the singular possessor book’s before it
the intervener carries its own singular finite verb (“a community that remains”), so the wrong number sounds right twice
plural key behind singular nouns; three singular distractors in present perfect, present and progressive

band7.why: Plural head behind the singular possessor “book’s” and three singular nouns, with an intervener verb of the other number (“remains”), as f10b7ce4; three singular distractors in three tenses.

items.subtype: Plural vs possessive nouns: two slots, plain plural then generic plural possessor with no article
items.passage: The echidna, a spine-covered insectivore of Australia and New Guinea, is one of the few mammals that reproduce by laying eggs. Because this monotreme lacks nipples, hatchlings obtain nourishment by licking milk from ______ skin, where it is secreted through dozens of specialized pores.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: Nothing belongs to the patches, so the plain plural “patches” is needed. The skin belongs to echidna females in general (the passage speaks of echidna “hatchlings” in general, even though it opens with the generic singular “The echidna”), so the plural possessive “females’” is correct.

A.recipe: needless apostrophe on a plain plural
A.why_wrong: “Patch’s” is a singular possessive, but nothing belongs to the patches; the plain plural “patches” is needed.

B.why_wrong: “Female’s” is a singular possessive with no article, but the skin belongs to echidna females in general, so the plural possessive “females’” is needed.

C.why_wrong: “Females” is a plain plural; the possessive “females’” is needed to show that the skin belongs to the females.

items.notes: Subject: natural science (echidnas feed their young from milk patches, having no nipples). No named researchers. Options as in 2784cbaf; key not the longest.
band7_moves: two slots with a generic plural possessor and no article, as 2784cbaf (objects’ movement)

the generic singular “The echidna” and “this monotreme” pull toward the singular possessor, as “an object” does in 2784cbaf, while the generic plural “hatchlings” keeps the plural possessor natural; “females” rather than a kinship noun, so a bare singular possessor with no article has no defensible reading
option grid as 2784cbaf: needless apostrophe, singular possessor, missing apostrophe

band7.why: Same two-slot grid as 2784cbaf, the only band-7 R6 grid item: generic plural possessor with no article, and after the fix a generic singular earlier in the passage pulling toward the singular. Passage 42 words, above the 28-word model but under the hard-tier median.

fixes: hardened: the opener was plural (“Echidnas ... these monotremes”), so every number cue pointed to the key; now the generic singular “The echidna ... this monotreme” pulls toward “female’s,” as “an object” does in 2784cbaf

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement: singular head (use) behind a dash interrupter full of plural nouns, be-family options
items.passage: In the 1500s, ceramicists in the Ottoman town of Iznik produced glazed tiles for many of Istanbul’s most magnificent mosques. Their use of a brilliant red pigment—derived from an iron-rich clay known as Armenian bole and applied to tulips, carnations, and other floral motifs so thickly that it projects slightly above the surrounding glaze—______ a technical achievement that subsequent potters struggled to replicate.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject of the second sentence is the singular noun “use,” not the plural nouns inside the dashes (“tulips, carnations, and other floral motifs”). The singular verb “was” agrees with it.

B.why_wrong: “Were” is plural and does not agree with the singular subject “use.”

C.why_wrong: “Have been” is plural and does not agree with the singular subject “use.”

D.why_wrong: “Are” is plural and does not agree with the singular subject “use.”

items.notes: Subject: arts and history (Iznik tiles, raised red made from Armenian bole). No named people. About 30 words between head and blank, three plural nouns right before the dash closes.

band7.why: Singular head behind a long dash interrupter full of plural nouns, as band-6 ea0aa676; the interrupter’s own verb (“projects”) has the head’s number, so it does not add the band-7 opposite-number trap.

fixes: head noun “application” changed to “use” (“application of a pigment ... applied to” was redundant); explanation updated

items.subtype: Finite vs nonfinite: second verb of a compound predicate (published ... but ___), split from the first by a dash pair
items.passage: In 1895, physicist Jagadish Chandra Bose used very short radio waves, now called microwaves, to ring a bell at a distance during a public demonstration in Calcutta (now Kolkata). He later published detailed descriptions of the devices he had built for such experiments—horn antennas and waveguides among them—but ______ to patent them, believing that scientific knowledge should be freely shared.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The blank is the second verb of the compound predicate that begins “He later published,” joined by “but.” It needs a finite past-tense verb, “declined,” to match the clause’s past-tense narration and complete the predicate.

A.recipe: nonfinite where a finite verb is needed (-ing)
A.why_wrong: The -ing form “declining” cannot serve as the second main verb after “but”; the sentence needs a finite verb.

B.recipe: nonfinite where a finite verb is needed (to + base)
B.why_wrong: The infinitive “to decline” cannot serve as the second main verb after “but”; the sentence needs a finite verb.

D.recipe: nonfinite where a finite verb is needed (having + past participle)
D.why_wrong: “Having declined” is a participle and cannot serve as the second main verb after “but”; the sentence needs a finite verb.

items.notes: Subject: history of science (J. C. Bose, 1895 microwave demonstration in Calcutta; he declined to patent his devices). Real figure, known. Planned as band 7, written as a strong band 6 with band_target 6: R2_finite_second has no band-7 official item (spec/rw/band7/form_structure_and_sense.md appendix). Head “He” sits about 25 words before the blank, past a dash pair with plural nouns.

band7.why: R2_finite_second has no band-7 official items (band-7 doc appendix), so it cannot be band 7; a strong band 6 like b74f676f, with the head 25 words back past a dash pair.

items.subtype: Pronoun-antecedent agreement: plural subject pronoun; a singular generic antecedent (The bichir) in the previous sentence tempts “it”
items.passage: The bichir, an African freshwater fish equipped with a pair of primitive lungs, can also propel itself across land using its pectoral fins. When a research team in Canada raised juvenile bichirs on land for eight months, ______ walked more efficiently than bichirs raised in aquariums, positioning their fins closer to their bodies.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The pronoun refers to the plural noun phrase “juvenile bichirs,” the fish that were raised on land, so the plural pronoun “they” is needed; “their fins” and “their bodies” later in the sentence confirm the plural.

A.recipe: wrong number pronoun (attractor in previous sentence)
A.why_wrong: “It” is singular and could only point back to “The bichir” in the first sentence or to “a research team,” but the fish that walked more efficiently are the plural “juvenile bichirs.”

C.why_wrong: “This” is singular and does not agree with the plural antecedent “juvenile bichirs.”

D.why_wrong: “We” is first person, but the sentence refers to the fish, “juvenile bichirs,” which call for the third-person “they.”

items.notes: Subject: natural science (bichirs raised on land walk more efficiently, Polypterus, 2014 study in Canada). No named researchers. Attractors: the singular generic “The bichir” opens the passage and “a research team” is singular, so “juvenile bichirs” is the only plural candidate, as “the Mississippi” tempts “it” in 2.4.

review.notes: “it” could reach for “a research team,” but “their fins” and “their bodies” later in the sentence rule it out

items.subtype: Plural vs possessive nouns: singular possessor + plural noun, partial grid
items.passage: After relocating to Paris in 1970, Lebanese painter Huguette Caland embarked on Bribes de corps (Body Parts), a series of sensual, brightly colored canvases. Many of the ______ in the series magnify the contours of the human body so dramatically that they initially resemble abstract landscapes.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The paintings belong to one artist, Huguette Caland, so the singular possessive “artist’s” is needed. Nothing belongs to the paintings, so the plain plural “paintings” is correct.

A.why_wrong: “Artists” is a plain plural; the singular possessive “artist’s” is needed to show that the paintings belong to Caland.

B.recipe: needless apostrophe on a plain plural
B.why_wrong: “Painting’s” is a singular possessive, but the sentence needs the plain plural “paintings”; nothing belongs to the paintings.

D.recipe: wrong possessor number plus needless apostrophe
D.why_wrong: “Artists’” is a plural possessive, but the paintings belong to a single artist, and “paintings’” wrongly adds a possessive to a plain plural.

items.notes: Subject: arts (Huguette Caland, Bribes de corps, 1970s). Number cue for the possessor: the single painter named in the first sentence.

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement: singular head (prefix) behind a dash interrupter full of plural nouns, lexical-verb options
items.passage: Like other Bantu languages, Zulu, spoken mainly in South Africa, organizes its nouns into grammatical classes. The prefix attached to a noun—um- for many words designating a single person, aba- for their plurals, and a dozen or so others for categories such as trees, instruments, and abstract concepts—______ the forms of the adjectives, verbs, and pronouns that refer to it.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject of the second sentence is the singular noun “prefix,” not the plural nouns inside the dashes (“words,” “plurals,” “others,” “categories”). The singular verb “determines” agrees with it.

A.why_wrong: “Determine” is plural and does not agree with the singular subject “prefix.”

B.why_wrong: “Are determining” is plural and does not agree with the singular subject “prefix.”

C.why_wrong: “Have determined” is plural and does not agree with the singular subject “prefix.”

items.notes: Subject: social science, linguistics (Zulu noun-class prefixes um- and aba- and agreement). No named people.

items.subtype: Modifier placement: preposition + gerund opener (In compiling), passage-final clause; plain agent key
items.passage: In 921 CE, the Abbasid caliph in Baghdad sent a diplomatic mission to the ruler of the Volga Bulgars, whose territory lay along trade routes also frequented by the Rus, merchants of Scandinavian origin. In compiling an account of the expedition, ______
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: Ahmad ibn Fadlan, a member of the mission, included one of the earliest detailed descriptions of the Rus.
one of the earliest detailed descriptions of the Rus was included by Ahmad ibn Fadlan, a member of the mission.
the work of Ahmad ibn Fadlan, a member of the mission, included one of the earliest detailed descriptions of the Rus.
it was Ahmad ibn Fadlan, a member of the mission, who included one of the earliest detailed descriptions of the Rus.
items.explanation: The person who compiled an account of the expedition was Ahmad ibn Fadlan. Choice A places “Ahmad ibn Fadlan” immediately after the opening phrase, so the phrase correctly describes him.

B.recipe: passive that leaves the wrong noun as subject (V)
B.why_wrong: “One of the earliest detailed descriptions” follows the phrase, so the sentence illogically says that a description compiled an account of the expedition.

C.why_wrong: The subject is “the work,” so the sentence illogically says that a piece of writing compiled the account.

D.why_wrong: The word “it” follows the phrase, so the phrase has no logical noun to describe; the person who compiled the account must be the subject.

items.notes: Subject: history (Ahmad ibn Fadlan, Abbasid embassy to the Volga Bulgars, 921 to 922; his account describes the Rus). Real figure, known. Options 17 to 19 words; key the shortest.

items.subtype: Modifier placement: past participial opener (Translated into), mid-sentence blank; right subject is a possessive + noun (Wong’s 1950 memoir)
items.passage: Raised in San Francisco’s Chinatown, Jade Snow Wong gained recognition both as a ceramicist and as an author. Translated into several Asian languages through a State Department initiative, ______ audiences far beyond the United States, and Wong later undertook a four-month lecture tour of Asia.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: Wong wrote a 1950 memoir, Fifth Chinese Daughter, that reached
there was a 1950 memoir by Wong, Fifth Chinese Daughter, that reached
Wong’s 1950 memoir, Fifth Chinese Daughter, reached
the State Department helped Wong’s 1950 memoir, Fifth Chinese Daughter, reach
items.explanation: What was “translated into several Asian languages” was a book, not a person or an agency. Choice C places “Wong’s 1950 memoir” immediately after the opening phrase, so the phrase correctly describes the memoir.

A.recipe: wrong noun as subject (W): the author
A.why_wrong: “Wong” follows the phrase, so the sentence illogically says that Wong herself was translated into several Asian languages.

B.why_wrong: The word “there” follows the phrase, leaving the phrase without a logical noun to describe.

D.recipe: wrong noun as subject (W): the agency
D.why_wrong: “The State Department” follows the phrase, so the sentence illogically says that the government agency was translated into several Asian languages.

items.notes: Subject: literature (Jade Snow Wong, Fifth Chinese Daughter, 1950; State Department translations and a lecture tour of Asia in 1953). Real figure, known. Key the shortest option, a possessive + noun as in 2.19.

items.subtype: Finite vs nonfinite: -ing participial result phrase after a complete clause and a comma
items.passage: Peruvian soprano Yma Sumac was celebrated for a vocal range that critics described as spanning more than four octaves. Her performances of songs inspired by Andean folk traditions attracted large audiences in New York during the late 1940s, ______ her a recording contract with Capitol Records in 1950.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The clause before the comma is already complete, with the subject “Her performances” and the verb “attracted.” The blank begins a phrase that adds a result, so the nonfinite participle “winning” is needed.

A.recipe: finite where a nonfinite phrase is needed
A.why_wrong: “Won” makes a second main verb joined to “attracted” by only a comma, which is not standard.

C.recipe: finite where a nonfinite phrase is needed
C.why_wrong: “Was winning” is finite and makes a second main verb joined to “attracted” by only a comma, which is not standard.

D.recipe: finite where a nonfinite phrase is needed
D.why_wrong: “Wins” is finite and makes a second main verb joined to “attracted” by only a comma, which is not standard.

items.notes: Subject: arts, music (Yma Sumac, Peruvian soprano, Capitol Records contract in 1950). Real figure, known; only widely reported facts.

items.subtype: Pronoun-antecedent agreement: singular object pronoun, antecedent the subject of the previous clause
items.passage: Korean American author Younghill Kang published his novel East Goes West in 1937. Chronicling a young Korean immigrant’s efforts to establish himself in New York, the book draws heavily on its author’s own life, and many literary historians consider ______ one of the first major works of Asian American fiction.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The pronoun refers to the singular noun phrase “the book,” Kang’s novel East Goes West, so the singular pronoun “it” is needed.

A.why_wrong: “Them” is plural and does not agree with the singular antecedent “the book.”

B.why_wrong: “These” is plural and does not agree with the singular antecedent “the book.”

C.why_wrong: “Those” is plural and does not agree with the singular antecedent “the book.”

items.notes: Subject: literature (Younghill Kang, East Goes West, 1937). Real work, known; no claims beyond its setting and standing.

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement: plural head right before the blank behind a short phrase, be-family options
items.passage: Although they are members of the hyena family, aardwolves seldom consume meat. These solitary, nocturnal animals of eastern and southern Africa ______ highly specialized insectivores, capable of consuming as many as 300,000 termites in a single night with their broad, sticky tongues.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject of the second sentence is the plural noun “animals.” The plural verb “are” agrees with it.

A.why_wrong: “Is” is singular and does not agree with the plural subject “animals.”

B.why_wrong: “Was” is singular and does not agree with the plural subject “animals.”

D.why_wrong: “Has been” is singular and does not agree with the plural subject “animals.”

items.notes: Subject: natural science (aardwolves, termite-eating members of the hyena family). No named people.

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement: singular named subject + appositive, be-family options
items.passage: W. Arthur Lewis, an economist from the Caribbean island of Saint Lucia, ______ awarded a share of the 1979 Nobel Prize in Economic Sciences. His influential model explains how workers in developing economies shift from agriculture into manufacturing and how that transition drives economic growth.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject of the first sentence is the singular noun “W. Arthur Lewis,” and the phrase between the commas only describes him. The singular verb “was” agrees with it.

B.why_wrong: “Were” is plural and does not agree with the singular subject “W. Arthur Lewis.”

C.why_wrong: “Are” is plural and does not agree with the singular subject “W. Arthur Lewis.”

D.why_wrong: “Have been” is plural and does not agree with the singular subject “W. Arthur Lewis.”

items.notes: Subject: social science, economics (W. Arthur Lewis, 1979 Nobel Prize in Economic Sciences, model of labor moving from agriculture to industry). Real figure, known.

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement: plural head right before the blank, lexical-verb options
items.passage: The compass plant (Silphium laciniatum), a towering wildflower of North American prairies, owes its name to an unusual growth pattern. Its large, deeply lobed leaves ______ to orient themselves vertically, with their flat surfaces facing east and west and their edges pointing north and south.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject of the second sentence is the plural noun “leaves.” The plural verb “tend” agrees with it.

A.why_wrong: “Tends” is singular and does not agree with the plural subject “leaves.”

C.why_wrong: “Is tending” is singular and does not agree with the plural subject “leaves.”

D.why_wrong: “Has tended” is singular and does not agree with the plural subject “leaves.”

items.notes: Subject: natural science (compass plant, Silphium laciniatum, leaves held edge-on north and south). No named people.

items.subtype: Finite vs nonfinite: missing main verb after the subject
items.passage: Linear Elamite, a script used in what is now Iran more than 4,000 years ago, resisted decipherment for over a century after the first inscriptions were found. In 2022, a team led by archaeologist François Desset ______ that it had worked out the sounds of most of the script’s signs.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The second sentence needs a main verb for its subject, “a team.” The finite past-tense verb “announced” supplies it.

A.recipe: nonfinite where a finite verb is needed (having + past participle)
A.why_wrong: “Having announced” is a participle, so the sentence would have no main verb.

B.recipe: nonfinite where a finite verb is needed (-ing)
B.why_wrong: “Announcing” is a participle, so the sentence would have no main verb.

C.recipe: nonfinite where a finite verb is needed (to + base)
C.why_wrong: “To announce” is an infinitive, so the sentence would have no main verb.

items.notes: Subject: social science and history, linguistics (decipherment of Linear Elamite announced in 2022). Real team leader named for a widely reported claim; the passage says only that the team announced it.

items.subtype: Finite vs nonfinite: missing main verb (be) after a short opener and the subject
items.passage: Around 1957, a boy exploring his family’s farm near Lydenburg, South Africa, noticed fragments of pottery eroding from a gully. Archaeologists later reassembled the pieces into seven hollow terracotta heads. Made around 500 CE, the Lydenburg Heads ______ among the earliest known sculptures from southern Africa.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The second sentence needs a main verb for its subject, “the Lydenburg Heads.” The finite verb “are” supplies it.

A.recipe: nonfinite where a finite verb is needed (having + past participle)
A.why_wrong: “Having been” is a participle, so the sentence would have no main verb.

B.recipe: nonfinite where a finite verb is needed (to + base)
B.why_wrong: “To be” is an infinitive, so the sentence would have no main verb.

D.recipe: nonfinite where a finite verb is needed (-ing)
D.why_wrong: “Being” is a participle, so the sentence would have no main verb.

items.notes: Subject: arts and archaeology (the Lydenburg Heads, terracotta heads made around 500 CE, South Africa). The finder is not named.

fixes: passage: “a gully, which archaeologists later reassembled” attached the relative clause to “gully”; split into two sentences

items.subtype: Tense: simple present for a general habit, cued by the present verbs around it
items.passage: Whirligig beetles swim in rapid, looping circles on the surfaces of freshwater ponds and streams. Because each of their compound eyes is divided into an upper and a lower section, a beetle can simultaneously watch for predators in the air and underwater as it ______ along.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The passage describes what whirligig beetles generally do, using present-tense verbs such as “swim,” “is divided” and “can ... watch.” The simple present “glides” matches this general description.

B.recipe: simple past where present is needed
B.why_wrong: “Glided” places the action in the past, but the passage describes a present, general habit.

C.recipe: past perfect where present is needed
C.why_wrong: “Had glided” places the action before another past event, but the passage describes a present, general habit.

D.why_wrong: “Will have glided” refers to an action completed by a future time, but the passage describes a present, general habit.

items.notes: Subject: natural science (whirligig beetles, eyes split into upper and lower sections). No named people.

items.subtype: Plural vs possessive nouns: full 2 x 2 grid, singular possessor + plural noun
items.passage: Japanese naturalist Minakata Kumagusu spent decades collecting slime molds and fungi in the forests of the Kii Peninsula, documenting each find with careful notes and detailed drawings. Many of the ______ are still preserved in museum collections that researchers consult today.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The specimens belong to one naturalist, Minakata Kumagusu, so the singular possessive “naturalist’s” is needed. Nothing belongs to the specimens, so the plain plural “specimens” is correct.

A.why_wrong: “Naturalists” is a plain plural; the singular possessive “naturalist’s” is needed to show that the specimens belong to Minakata.

C.recipe: needless apostrophe on a plain plural
C.why_wrong: “Specimen’s” is a singular possessive, but the sentence needs the plain plural “specimens”; nothing belongs to the specimens.

D.recipe: missing apostrophe on the possessor plus needless apostrophe
D.why_wrong: “Naturalists” lacks the apostrophe the possessor needs, and “specimen’s” wrongly makes a plain plural possessive.

items.notes: Subject: natural science and history (Japanese naturalist Minakata Kumagusu, slime molds and fungi of the Kii Peninsula). Real figure, known.

items.subtype: Plural vs possessive nouns: 2 x 2 grid, singular possessor (the ship) + plural noun
items.passage: Archaeologists have reconstructed many techniques of ancient Greek shipbuilding by studying the Kyrenia ship, a merchant vessel that sank off the northern coast of Cyprus around 300 BCE. The ______ were rapidly buried beneath sediment on the seafloor, which kept them remarkably well preserved until a sponge diver found the wreck in 1965.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The timbers belong to one ship, the Kyrenia ship, so the singular possessive “ship’s” is needed. Nothing belongs to the timbers, and the plural verb “were” shows there are many of them, so the plain plural “timbers” is correct.

A.why_wrong: “Ships” is a plain plural; the singular possessive “ship’s” is needed to show that the timbers belong to the Kyrenia ship.

B.recipe: wrong possessor number plus needless apostrophe
B.why_wrong: “Ships’” is a plural possessive, but the timbers belong to a single ship, and “timbers’” wrongly makes a plain plural possessive.

C.recipe: needless apostrophe on a plain plural
C.why_wrong: “Timber’s” is a singular possessive, but the sentence needs the plain plural “timbers”; nothing belongs to the timbers.

items.notes: Subject: history and archaeology (the Kyrenia ship, Greek merchant vessel that sank off Cyprus around 300 BCE). No named people.

items.subtype: Tense: past perfect for an action earlier than a dated past event (more than forty years earlier)
items.passage: In 1835, Swedish chemist Jöns Jacob Berzelius coined the term “catalysis” to describe how some substances speed up chemical reactions without being used up. Scottish chemist Elizabeth Fulhame, however, ______ the idea in a book published more than forty years earlier.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: Fulhame’s book appeared “more than forty years earlier” than Berzelius’s 1835 coinage, an action completed before another past event. The past perfect “had described” shows that order.

A.why_wrong: “Will have described” refers to the future, but Fulhame’s book was published in the past, before 1835.

C.recipe: present progressive where past perfect is needed
C.why_wrong: “Is describing” presents the action as happening now, but Fulhame’s book was published before 1835.

D.recipe: simple future where past perfect is needed
D.why_wrong: “Will describe” places the action in the future, but Fulhame’s book was published more than forty years before 1835.

items.notes: Subject: history of science (Elizabeth Fulhame’s 1794 essay on combustion described catalysis before Berzelius named it in 1835). Real figures, known.

fixes: options: C “describes” was defensible as the literary present for a book’s content, and D “was describing” was arguable; now “is describing” and “will describe,” as in model 588887b9

items.subtype: Finite vs nonfinite: second verb of a compound predicate joined by and
items.passage: Born in Africa around 1518, Juan Latino was enslaved as a child and taken to Granada, Spain, where he was educated alongside his enslaver’s son. He eventually earned a degree from the University of Granada and ______ Latin grammar at the city’s cathedral school, becoming one of Renaissance Spain’s most celebrated scholars.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The blank is the second verb of the compound predicate “earned ... and ______.” It must be a finite past-tense verb like “earned,” so “taught” is correct.

B.recipe: nonfinite where a finite verb is needed (-ing)
B.why_wrong: “Teaching” is a participle and cannot be joined by “and” to the finite verb “earned” as a second main verb.

C.recipe: nonfinite where a finite verb is needed (to + base)
C.why_wrong: “To teach” is an infinitive and cannot be joined by “and” to the finite verb “earned” as a second main verb.

D.recipe: nonfinite where a finite verb is needed (having + past participle)
D.why_wrong: “Having taught” is a participle and cannot be joined by “and” to the finite verb “earned” as a second main verb.

items.notes: Subject: history (Juan Latino, sixteenth-century Latin scholar in Granada). Real figure, known.
